newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Jailed Socialist boss urges all Albanians to vote.
newsitem.headline: Jailed Socialist boss urges all Albanians to vote.

text.p: Albania's jailed opposition Socialist leader Fatos Nano has urged his supporters not to boycott nationwide local elections next Sunday and said opposition parties must unite against the government.

The Socialist Party, the former communists, and most other opposition groups pulled out of a general election in May after accusing President Sali Berisha's ruling Democratic Party of vote-rigging and fraud.

"The whole Albanian electorate should take the fate of the nation in its hands on October 20 and give no space to the adventurism...of Berisha's regime," Nano told the leftist daily Zeri i Popullit in an interview published on Tuesday.
The interview was conducted in a jail in the remote southern Albanian town of Tepelena where Nano has spent the past two years behind bars.

"There is no other way out from the present crisis except through mass participation in the elections...mass monitoring, and the building of democratic institutions on the foundations of a free vote," Nano, a former prime minister, said.

Nano was jailed in 1994 on charges of embezzlement during his brief stint as prime minister in 1991 and still has more than two years to serve. International human rights groups have called for his release, claiming that his trial was flawed.
Nano said the Democrats could not be wholly blamed for the current state of the country but said the government had failed to stick to pledges it made in its manifesto.
The opposition wanted to push on with economic reform, halt human rights violations and fight corruption and organised crime, he added.

International monitors criticised the conduct of the two-round general election in May and June. The United States has advised Berisha on more than one occasion to hold a fresh general election as soon as possible.
Berisha's Democrats, who won nearly all seats in the parliament in the disputed general election, had accused the Socialists of trying to organise a boycott of local polls.
But the Socialists and other opposition parties abandoned earlier threats of a boycott, despite alleging that the Democrats were once again attempting to rig electoral lists.
Council of Europe observers arrived in Albania this week to monitor the local elections, considered by many Western states to be a crucial test of the Balkan state's young democracy.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the strongest critic of the general election, is still awaiting permission from the Albanian government to despatch its monitors.
